speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:

I wish to rise to a question of privilege, having regard to the answers given by the hon. Postmaster General to certain questions asked to-day by the hon. member for Peterborough East (Mr. Sexsmith) with regard to an official trip I made in 1911. I do not take objection to all of the answers, but, in order to elucidate matters, some little explanation is required on my part with regard to one or two of them. The first question is as follows:
Who accompanied the Hon. Mr. Lemieux on his Asiatic trip?
The answer to this is absolutely correct:
His private secretary, the Under Secretary of State and his secretary.
The second and third questions are:
How many stenographers accompanied him or were employed by him or his staff, and at what cost?
How many servants or valets were in or were engaged for the party?
The very able answer given by my hon. friend is as follows:
The department has no official knowledge about this.
I say that my hon. friend could have had the information for this, as he had for the other questions, from my secretary, who is still in the employ of his department; and my hon. friend, in courtesy to myself, would have been able to answer that there were no servants, no valets and no stenographers except my private secretary, as my hon. friend answered question one.
Question 5 reads:
Were the expenses of the said ladies or any portion thereof, paid by the Government of Canada, directly or indirectly.
To this the reply was:
There is nothing in the department about this.
I say this answer is not clear, and my hon. friend should have been able to ascertain from my private secretary, who is still in the employ of the department, if any moneys were paid for ladies accompanying

the Postmaster General on that trip. To questions 7 and 8, I have nothing to say, except that if my hon. friend would inquire from the gentleman who was my private secretary at the time, he would know that there were contributions, not from the Imperial Government of Great Britain, but from the Government of Japan, in connection with that trip. I want to elucidate this matter so as to leave no doubt in the minds of hon. gentlemen.

I rise to a question of privilege in respect to the taking of to-day (Thursday) as a Government day. I raise this question owing to the fact that there are many Public Bills now on the Order Paper that may not be reached again this session. In the session of 1910, November 17 was the opening day and I presented my Eight-hour Bill for its second reading on the 15th of December, which was the fifth Thursday of the session. On the previous night the leader of the Government to-day, who was then leader of the Opposition, asked the minister who was leading the House, Hon. Wm. Paterson, about this matter, and he was told by Mr. Paterson that the next day was not a Government day. The right hon. leader of the Opposition will find that at page 1338 of the ' Hansard ' of 1910. At page 1407 of the same volume he will find the report of the second reading of the Eight-hour Bill. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
As I was consulted

I am informed that the arrangement made with the province of Manitoba is that they pay $5,000 a year. There was a question asked about recruiting. I am prepared with the information on that point if hon. gentlemen would like it. It is contained in the following memorandum which has been furnished me by the comptroller:
It has been extremely difficult during the last two or three years to obtain recruits in Canada, nothwithstanding the increased rates of pay.
In April, 1912, recruiting was carried on in Winnipeg for one month resulting in the acceptance of only 11 men out of 75 applicants.
About the same time an officer was employed recruiting in Ontario for a couple of months and engaged only 26 men, 19 of whom were obtained in Toronto,-the rest of western Ontario furnishing only 7.
An officer was also sent to the Maritime provinces who secured 26 men in Nova SCotia, but' none in New Brunswick.
Recruiting posters were sent to every post office within a radius of 50 miles of Ottawa, but no application for engagement resulted therefrom.
Prom the foregoing it will be seen that notwithstanding due notice of the recruiting having

been given by the distribution of posters throughout the towns and advertisements in the local newspapers, only 63 men were accepted for service throughout the whole of Canada, as a result of this recruiting. A few more men were engaged from time to time at Regina and Ottawa.
An officer being on leave in England during the summer of 1912 was instructed to secure from 25 to 30 men as an experiment and he brought out 29 men, who either paid their own expenses, or agreed to repay the advances made by the Government.
In the spring of 1913, the force being about 100 under strength, recruiting was carried on in Winnipeg for over a month and only 23 men were engaged. It was then decided to recruit in England and in the month of July 98 men of a very superior class were engaged, out of about 1,300 applicants, and sent to Regina, the Government advancing the transport, the men repaying the cost of the journey from Quebec to Regina, namely, $27.98,-that from London to Quebec $24.33 being borne by the police appropriation.
During the year 1913, 259 recruits were accepted for service, 161 of whom were engaged in Canada and 98 in Great Britain.
Of the 161 engaged in Canada 19 only were Canadian born, 127 being natives of the old country, a large number of whom came out to join the force after the engagement of recruits in London. Of the balance of the 259, 6 were born in India, 4 in the United States, and 1 each in Jamaica, Australia, Prance, Germany and Denmark.
The force is now up to its full strength, namely, 760, and the engagement of men in England last summer has resulted in a continual flow of applications from young men of good education, well fitted for the work, who are willing to come out to Canada at their own expense to join the force.
Attached hereto is a statement showing the countries of birth of recruits engaged during the calendar years 1912 and 1913.
Respectfully submitted.

They were carefully selected and a fine lot physically; 45 were old soldiers, a large proportion from the Guards and Cavalry. All promised to be very serviceable members of the force.
The present conditions of recruiting are excellent. Applications are received daily. Only those of apparently superior merit are accepted. I attribute this to improved conditions, to the very substantial increase of pay granted this year and the lack of suitable civil employment.
Some time ago my right hon. friend said there was insufficient recruiting for the Mounted Police. I was surprised at that statement and looked up the report, and I found my case strengthened by the statement there that there is no difficulty in securing recruits; that the present conditions of recruiting are excellent; that applications are received daily, and that only those of superior merit are accepted.
Recruiting in England is very valuable because among the ex-army men there can be found candidates admirably suited for the service. An equally as good source of recruiting, however, is to be found among our young Canadians, many of whom are always ready to enter this adventurous service. I wish it were even better known than at the present, that the Royal Northwest Mounted Police service affords a very attractive opening for young men of courage, good physique, and intelligence. If

young man enters the force at the age of twenty, after twenty years' service, when he is still a comparatively young man, he receives a pension, which though not large, is sufficient to support him. He knows the country thoroughly; he has had occasion to patrol it, and to see it from the American boundary to the Arctic ocean, and consequently he can settle down where his enterprise may lead him. For these reasons the force has always been rather popular.

fSir Wilfrid Laurier.]

While it is easier to secure a sufficient enlistment by opening recruiting offices in England, I do not think the results in the efficiency of [DOT] the force are going to be as satisfactory as if the recruiting was carried on solely in Canada; quite irrespective of the fact of whether the recruit is of Canadian or of British birth. If a man has left his original home in the British Isles on his own initiative and has fought his own way in Canada for a greater or lesser period thereby becoming familiar with the conditions of life and with the people, I would consider him to be very much more eligible and better fitted for the work than if, never having shown that initiative, he has enlisted in England, and is without any previous knowledge of Canadian conditions. Just in proportion as it is easier to get men on the other side, are those men liable not to be as efficient after entering upon their duties as if they had been enlisted on this side, after a residence in Canada.
The Mounted Police force differs radically from a military force. In a military force, until very recent years at any rate, obedience, conformity to discipline, was the great requirement, but in the Mounted Police force where men are operating at vast distances from headquarters, perhaps individually or with only a very small number and with, possibly, only a very subordinate officer in charge, unless they have individual initiative-which no training can supply but which must be in a man to begin with, to be developed-they cannot act with desired efficiency. I wish to place these views strongly before the minister for his consideration.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I appreciate what has been said by my hon. friend, but I would like him to remember that recruiting was not undertaken in England until every reasonable effort had been exhausted in this country, efforts made not only in the West, but in Ontario and the Maritime provinces. I am informed by the Comptroller that the men who have recently come from England have made very satisfactory members of the force. I know that we are supposed to have in this country a people possessed of greater initiative than those of countries where conditions of life are more stereotyped; but I* think my hon. friend will remember that the native of the British Islands, when he has been tested, has been found possessed of very remarkable powers of initiative. The Civil Service of India contains many

examples of men scattered all over the country, at very great distances from headquarters or from those who can give them instructions, who have acted in times of urgency or danger in a way which forbids us to think that the natives of the British Islands are not possessed of a great initiative when the demand is made. We have recruited in the British Islands because it seemed necessary, and so far as my information goes, the result of that recruiting, up to the present time, has been absolutely satisfactory. The men are of good education, and perform their duties in a thoroughly capable and reliable manner. While I should be glad if more Canadians had been attracted by the inducements to join the force, I am bound to say that the results of recruiting in the British Islands are all that we could reasonably have expected.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
While no one would condemn the recruiting of the force in the British Islands at the same time I think we have a good recruiting ground in Canada. I should be far from discouraging recruiting in the British Islands. The men recruited there are chiefly old soldiers, and naturally would make excellent members of the force, but I do not think we could expect them to reach the standard of excellence of Canadians recruited very early in life. The example of the Civil Service of India is not at all apposite to the question. The members of the Indian Civil Service are sent to their work in their youth, after having received a special training for their duties, and, as all the world knows, they perform those duties most admirably. The fact that these young men direct the affairs of so many millions of people is the best testimony to their fitness; but the men who are brought over from England to serve in the Mounted Police are not of that character. If they are officers and men who have taken their discharge from the army, they must be relatively older, and, as the hon. member for Edmonton says, they have not the pliancy and the elasticity required in a constable of the Mounted Police. The Mounted Police constables, as my right hon. friend knows, must discharge not only the duties generally discharged by policemen, but duties of an infinitely varied character. Their best work is not so much seeing to the enforcement of the law and looking after offenders, but in rendering service to the settlers. If it has been deemed necessary to go to England for
recruits, I am glad that recruiting there has been so successful.
There is one thing to which I would call the attention of my right hon. friend. I see by the latest report of the Mounted Police that the number of crimes has largely increased in the three provinces in which the force operate, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, as might be expected, because with the large immigration, even though those immigrants be of the best element, such as are coming at the present time, there must be in a new community a greater number of crimes than in the old-settled portions of the country; but I notice with regret that there has been an increase in the number of the graver offences, especially murder. I do not know how far the administration of justice may be responsible but I observe also that there have been quite a number of commutations of the death sentence. We had a discussion the other day on the death penalty which I am sorry was not concluded, but, whatever opinion we may have formed on that subject, I am sure we must all hold that, so long as the law remains as it is and murder is punishable by death, then, only under the gravest possible circumstances should the sentence of the court be interfered with. I regret that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) is not in his place, but even in his absence I would call attention to cases referred to in which the sentence of death has been commuted. I read from the report, page 18, section 3:
Rex vs Bertrand. Convicted and sentenced to death; latterly commuted to life imprisonment. A cold-blooded case of uxoricide. He was charged with having murdered his wife at High River, Alta., by wilfully shooting her with a shotgun. It appears that Mrs. Bertrand owned certain property which her husband endeavoured to get control and possession of, but she steadily refused to let him get title or control. This matter seems to have been a bone of contention between them, leading to violent quarrels, and ultimately to the crime of which Bertrand was convicted.
This was a shocking crime; it is difficult to appreciate what reasons induced the Minister of Justice to recommend to clemency in this case. Tire next case is that of Rex vs. Verri:
Convicted and condemned to death, but latterly commuted to life imprisonment. A Calgary police case, result of drunken brawl. Verri stood indicted with the murder of another half-breed by name of Alfred Glenn. It appears that the former was intoxicated, quarrelled with his wife, went out of the tent in which he was living and announced that he was ready to fight any one. The late Alfred Glenn,

a neighbour who lived in an adjoining tent, and had nothing whatever to do with the family quarrel, stuck his head out of the flap of the tent to ascertain the cause of the trouble, whereupon Verrl smashed him on the head with a beer bottle, and inflicted serious injuries. Glenn was taken into hospital but succumbed in about ten days' time.
Here another horrible crime is reported, for which no possible excuse could be given on behalf of the convicted man. The next case is that of Rex vs. Stokely:
Convicted and condemned to death, but latterly commuted to life imprisonment.
Edwin Stokely stood charged with having wilfully shot and killed his brother, Frederick Stokely. They resided on adjoining quarter sections near Webber, Alta., and were recent arrivals from the United States. Bad blood seems to have existed between them for some time over certain family affairs, and to which, latterly, difficulties over money matters were added.
This is even more shocking than the others. The next case is that of Rex vs. Luzinski, a Galician:
Convicted and sentenced to death; latterly commuted to life imprisonment.
The body of an unknown man-afterwards identified as one Paul Malowski, a Galician in the employ of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, was found in small bluff covered with brush, within the town limits of Melville, Saskatchewan. The left side of deceased's face had evidently been struck with some heavy instrument, and the jpost 'mortem revealed that the jaw and cheek bones had been badly fractured. One of the Crown witnesses at the trial deposed that on Saturday evening, December 30, 1911, the accused persuaded Malowski to go with him on the pretext of visiting a farmer three miles away. Malowski at first demurred, because he said he had not suitable or sufficient clothes for the journey, and Luzinski thereupon lent him some of his own. The two men left together, and in about an hour afterwards Luzinski came back alone. He explained that they had met the party on the road, whom they went out to visit, and that Malowski drove on with the farmer, while he (Luzinski) turned back. Malowski was never seen alive again. It was known that Malowski was carrying a considerable sum of money on his person. Robbery was undoubtedly the motive of the crime, because, when the dead body of Malowski was discovered his pockets were rifled, and all his money and valuables missing.
In this case the evidence was evidently circumstantial, though it pointed strongly to the fact that Luzinski was the murderer. Still, there may have been something missing in the circumstances which induced the department to come to the conclusion that the prisoner ought to be given the benefit of the doubt, and that the sentence of death should not be carried out. But the other three cases, those of Bertrand, Verri and Stokely, seem to be cases of absolutely heinous murder, in respect of which nothing

could possibly be said in favour of the accused. It is admitted that the law in the western provinces, from the time the police force was established more than thirty years ago, has been most admirably carried out, and that the country has been comparatively free from crime. It is also apparent that the sight of the uniform has had a deterrent effect upon evil doers. There is no doubt but that the administration of the law has been just and merciful, and that where the court has come to the conclusion that a man is guilty, the penalty allotted by law should be carried out. But in these four oases there has been an interference with the sentence of the court. 1 do not want to attach any blame to the department, because there may have been good reasons for the course taken, but if there were good reasons they do not appear here, and it seems to me that some explanation should be made by my right hon. friend or by the Minister of Justice as to why these sentences were not carried out.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: With respect to the cases to which my right hon. friend has called attention, there are two of them that I do not at all recall, but as to the other two, I do recall the circumstances which were brought to our attention by the Minister of Justice.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Which were they?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I remember the case of Stokely and the case of Luzinski, but I do not remember them with sufficient clearness to discuss them. Indeed, I would not care to discuss them in the absence of the Minister of Justice, as certain principles have been laid down as to the discussion of such matters, the exact nature of which I do not recall at the moment, but from which I would not like to depart. My right hon. friend of course knows that in every one of such cases the presiding judge is consulted and makes a report, and a good deal of importance is attached to his recommendation. Although I do not intend to suggest-because I do not remember-that in all these cases there was any such recommendation from the judge, it is my impression that in at least one of the cases to which reference has been made there was such a recommendation. In some of the cases, if I remember correctly, the evidence was somewhat circumstantial.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The case of Luzinski?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes, and possibly one of the others. I would not like it to be understood, from the reading of the cases to which the right hon. gentleman has called attention, that so large a percentage of capital cases as would be suggested by the enumeration of these four, have resulted in commutation. In a great many of these cases the questions submitted to the consideration of the Minister of Justice are rather difficult, and, as has always been the case, the report to council is always carefully considered. I think our practice in that regard is different from that prevailing in Great Britain, because I believe that there these cases do not go before the Cabinet at all; I think they are dealt with by the Home Secretary. Here the practice is to have them considered in the first instance by an officer of the Department of Justice who has had large experience.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Who is that officer now?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Cote, I think; he has had a large experience in performing duties of that character. After he has made his report upon the case, not only his report but the whole of the evidence is read by the Minister of Justice himself, and if there has not already been a report from the judge who tried the case, that report is asked fox. In fact I know that the Minister of Justice has addressed letters to all the judges of the country asking that in every case such a report should be sent to him at the earliest possible moment, in order that certain delays which have taken place in a few instances may be avoided in the future. The Minister of Justice, upon consideration of Mr. Cote's report and of the evidence itself and of all that may be urged by any person on behalf of the man convicted, makes his report to Council, and then all these reports are very carefully considered in Council, and we endeavour to discharge what seems to be our plain duty in every case. Naturally in such matters those who are called upon to consider the question of commutation may not always entertain exactly the same opinion. The duty of deciding upon such cases is not only a very responsible but a very difficult one. I appreciate thoroughly the importance of what the right hon. gentleman has said as to the necessity of a strict adherence to the verdict of the jury and the sentence pronounced thereon. We have not departed from that principle except in cases where it seemed our manifest duty to do
so. I shall inform the Minister of Justice of the observations which the right hon. gentleman has made with regard to cases which have been mentioned, and ask him to give his consideration to what may properly be said in regard to them.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I have no doubt whatever that the advisers of His Excellency, no matter who they may be, in the advice which they give to His Excellency with regard to these extreme sentences of the law, are actuated only by their own honest and conscientious convictions. Indeed it would be horrible to suppose anything to the contrary. But even while this is a principle which is well known, I have known, in the course of my life, such advice to be discussed in Parliament and very seriously criticised. I do not want to find any fault in the present instance; but on looking over the report I find that we have four cases of brutal murder, and on the face of the report it is impossible to conceive, in at least three of the cases, what reasons could have existed to induce the Minister of Justice to advise the commuting of the sentence. In the fourth case, the Luzinsky case, the evidence was circumstantial, and while it strongly pointed to the man who was indicted, perhaps-there was in this case some link missing which did not satisfy the Minister of Justice that, after all, the case was beyond all doubt. I do not say this by way of criticism. This report goes to the whole country and upon the face of it there are four cases there which would appear to have been commuted without sufficient reason. I will be glad to hear, at some future date, what were the reasons of the Minister of Justice for advising commutation in such cases.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There was another case, the Stokely case, where there were very peculiar circumstances. It was a dispute over land, over a boundary as well as over cattle, and the evidence placed before us would indicate that both parties had gone armed to the scene of action. There was evidently a disposition on both sides to use firearms. The evidence rendered it uncertain, if I remember correctly, as to whether there was not a very strong attempt on both sides to get the opportunity to shoot first. That case was a very painful case. It was a quarrel between members of the same family.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Two brothers.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: And evidently both sides had been determined to use firearms if necessary for their purpose. There was also a good deal of conflicting evidence as to the facts in the case, and I am not clear as to what the recommendation of the judge was. However, there will be an opportunity of discussing that later.

If I might revert to the
views I expressed a little while ago in regard to the locality of recruiting of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police and the remarks of the Prime Minister, apparently what I said was misunderstood. My hon. friend seems to have thought that I was drawing a contrast between the respective ability of Canadians and old country men.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: As to initiative only.

I can quite see that my hon. friend was under a misapprehension. I was drawing attention to the difference in initiative between different classes of old country men. The old country man who has come out here on his own initiative has demonstrated his initiative by coming out here and rustling for himself for a period before entering the force. As I understood the return, the large majority of the members of the force at the date of the information read by the Prime Minister, were of that class, in the proportion of something like 75 Canadians to 400 old country men. The condition that my right hon. friend has mentioned of the large proportion of old country men in the force is not new. From the very inception of the force and all through its history, a very large proportion of its membership, and of the most distinguished members of the force, were old country men, men who had become apprenticed to the conditions of life here and who were therefore well fitted to discharge the duties required of them.
I speak of this, not for the purpose of mere discussion or argument, and I do not wish it understood that I make criticisms for the sake of criticism. I would like to have it understood that my only object is to secure the best possible result from the organization and efforts of the force.
I am compelled to suggest that if it was possible to recruit sufficient men in Canada for the force up to a certain date, and that after that date it ceased to be possible, there is prima facie evidence that there was a change of conditions in the force, that rendered it less desirable as a vocation. That may have been because of conditions outside the force, or because of con-

ditions inside the force. I draw the Prime Minister's attention to the point, for the purpose of suggesting to him the very great desirability of his dealing with this prima facie case, and finding out why, although up to a certain date, we had been able to get sufficient recruits in Canada-not all Canadian born it is true, but men who had Canadian experience-after a certain time we had to go outside of Canada to engage those with no Canadian experience, who had shown no individual initiative, and whose worth remained to be tried. It is desirable that there should be a careful examination in regard to that point. I wish to say further that there has been a serious increase in unpunished crime in the western provinces within recent years, the perpetrators not having been discovered. That also is a matter that should receive very, very, careful attention. It may be because of a change of conditions in the population of the provinces; it may be because of a lessening of efficiency in the force, and it may be because of the measure of divided authority that now exists as between the Dominion and the provinces. The arrangements as to the several responsibilities of the force as a force, and the responsibilities of the provinces, as responsible for the administration of law and paying for the upkeep of the force, may or may not be satisfactory, and such as lend themselves to efficiency. Or, is there a difficulty existing that in any way militates against the results that in former years were unquestioned, as the result of the direct administration of the mounted police force ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The executive or military head of the force is exactly the same as it has been for a number of years. The Commissioner is Mr. Perry, a man of long experience who has been at the head of the force for some ten years or more, and who has been a member of the force for some 32 years. I do not know of any reason why the force should seem less attractive than formerly, and I should suppose that failure to obtain a sufficient number of recruits in Canada under arrangements made by the Comptroller and the Commissioner, must have been due to the fact that other opportunities for useful activity proved more attractive. Recruiting in England was not undertaken until we had failed to obtain a sufficient number of men in Canada. Of the 225 men natives of the British Isles who were enlisted in 1913 I think that only 98 were actually engaged in the British Isles; the

remainder being engaged in Canada, although I am not at all sure that those men had been in this country for a very long time. From the reports which I read a moment ago, I gathered that a great many came over to this country in the hope of an opportunity to enlist. The Comptroller inform? me that many of them had been in this country, one or two years at the time of enlistment. Others, no doubt, only came over a short time before enlisting. With regard to the suggested friction or lack of harmony between the force and the provincial authorities who primarily are re-sponsiDle for the administration of justice in those provinces, no such friction or lack of harmony has been brought to my attention and the Comptroller informs me that nothing of the kind has been brought to his attention by the Commissioner. In the absence of evidence to the contrary I am disposed to think that it does not exist.

I would like to impress
this point because the credit of the force and the credit of Canada is very deeply involved.- We have always prided ourselves upon the maintenance of law and order and the punishment of crime, particularly of serious crime, in the western provinces. When we find a condition in which, to an increasing degree, serious crime is unpunished the matter certainly calls for consideration and a search for whatever the cause may be.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Is my hon. friend referring to cases where the author of crime has not been detected?
Yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: And no arrest made?

Yes. The reason I ask as to the division of authority is that in the city of Edmonton, in the year 1912, a murder was committed; a woman was shot in her house and the perpetrator of the crime was never discovered. During the past summer a man named Hargraves was found murdered on the street and a man named McNulty was shot in his house. The perpetrators of these crimes were never discovered. I quite realize that primarily the responsibility rests upon the police of the town but, generally speaking, it rests upon the provincial authorities and I presume that in general -the police force is called into question. If there is any friction, if there is any division of responsibility that tends to prevent the effective discovery of crime, it should be searched out and done away with. If there is no
such disability, then, certainly the reason is all the greater why every consideration should be given to these terrible instances; because what has occurred in Edmonton is only what is occurring elsewhere. It is a feature of present conditions that the perpetrators of serious crimes are not discovered in the same proportion as prevailed in former days. If it is a question of jurisdiction or division of authority, let it be searched out and done away with in some way or another and let some readjustment be made. If it is a question of efficiency, that should be attended to. This changed condition is serious and I take this opportunity of bringing the attention of the Prime Minister and of the Government to it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I shall send the hon.
gentleman's observations to the Commissioner and ask him if he has anything to offer in regard to the situation Which the hon. gentleman describes. If there is any friction, or lack of -harmony, or division of responsibility, that has brought about any such results as are suggested, I certainly want to know that fact and to find a remedy -for it if it can be found. Up to the present nothing of the kind -has come to my attention. Should it come to my attention I will endeavour to provide a remedy.

The right hon. gentleman has given us the information as to the manner in which recruiting is carried on I would like to inquire how vacancies among the officers are filled. Is it by promotion or by bringing in others from the outside?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: In some cases by promotion, and m some case- by the appointment of persons who are not in the force. I think the rule generally observed has been that at least -half, and generally more than half, of the appointments to inspectorships are made from the force itself.
Has it been the custom for a certain number of years, when a vacancy occurs in the department at Ottawa, to bring in a person from the staff of officers to fill such vacancy?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No. Nothing of that
kind has ever been done, and 5 p.m. the Comptroller informs me that it would be impracticable because these officers are under different pension enactments.

While there have been a considerable proportion of promotions from

the ranks of the non-commissioned officers to the commissioned officers, there have been a number of appointments of officers from the outside. That does not tend towards the retention of the best men in the force, nor does it tend to attract capable, ambitious and useful men from the outside. It may be said by my right hon. friend that the late Government, as their predecessors, on occasion appointed men from the outside to the force. At that time it was possible to recruit sufficiently for the force in Canada. Conditions, for some reason or other, have changed, and I would respectfully suggest that one improvement that might be made by the Government would be to let it be thoroughly understood that commissions in the Mounted Police force are available only to members of the force who have earned them by merit.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The Comptroller informs me that there have been about 12 appointments-I am not speaking with absolute accuracy-to inspectorships since the office has been under my administration, and that all have been filled from the force itself except two. I also gather that about a similar proportion to that prevailed under the Administration of my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition. I mentioned a little while ago that at least half were filled from the force. Of course, the proportion is much greater than that- about five-sixths have been filled from the force according to the figures which I have just given to my hon. friend.

I believe it would have
a good effect if the Prime Minister were to anounce as a measure of policy that hereafter commissions in the force would be filled from amongst the non-commissioned officers.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Yes. It sometimes happens that there is an opportunity to appoint some one from outside of the force who seems to possess the most excellent qualifications for the purpose. It sometimes happens that it is a little difficult to appoint from within the force on account of a question of seniority, or in view of the fact that persons who may be considered to have very strong claims by reason of length of service are perhaps a little advanced in years and have not the vigor and initiative which may be desired for certain posts on the force. Considerations of that kind have been urged upon me I think, in the two cases to which I have

alluded, and these appointments were made from outside of the force for special rea-* sons.
I do not wish to suggest that the appointments made from outside may not be very meritorious.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I understand my hon.
friend.

The fact that they are
made from the outside has the effect upon the esprit of the force that my right hon. friend has mentioned.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I appreciate what my hon. friend has stated.
Royal Northwest Mounted Police-To compensate members of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police for Injuries received while in the discharge of duty, $3,000.

So far as the matter has come to my attention in the past, the compensation paid for injuries received has hardly been on a scale proportionate to the injury suffered. I may be wrong in that, but that is the impression I have gathered. I think the department would be well advised to make liberal compensation to men who have suffered injury in the discharge of their duty, to the extent of liberal provision for closely dependent relatives in case of death or disablement resulting from such injury. The occasion may arise at any moment when a policeman must face death. He must take his choice between the discharge of his duty and his possible permanent disablement or the loss of his life. While there is no money compensation that will ever put the spirit of sacrifice into a man-if it is not there already it will not be there when the crisis comes-at the same time I think the country can well afford to let its servants know that the country at large has an interest with them in the discharge of their duty and is prepared to show that interest by liberal provision in the ease of disablement or death, by provision for closely dependent relatives on a scale not based upon the conditions of a regular army in a European country, but based upon the conditions of life as they exist in this country and based further on the fact that the man who faces this danger does it, not because of discipline, not because he has been told to walk in a certain direction under a certain order, but with a full appreciation of the consequences to himself and simply because he has the highest regard for the duty that he has undertaken to perform.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I will bear in mind what my hon. friend has mentioned. If he will send me the names of the persons to whom he alludes, I shall be very glad to have their claims considered.

I am not speaking of a particular case; I am speaking generally. I am asking for information as to what the scale of compensation is. Is there any consideration for the widow of a constable killed in the discharge of his duty, and what is it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes. The Commissioner informs me that the pension to a widow amounts to one-half of the pay of the man who has been killed. In some cases, as my hon. friend knows, special compensation has been voted by Parliament, for example, in the case of Inspector Fitzgerald.

Within the year some of the constables at Edmonton were required to arrest a settler who had suddenly become insane. One, if not two of them, were killed in making the arrest. I do not know if they left any dependents, blit if they did, it was a case that came very close home. A constable, if he is to be efficient, must make up his mind on the instant as to whether he is to face death or disablement or not, and I think the country should be substantially behind him in that very difficult circumstance.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I agree with my hon. friend. In the case to which the hon. gentleman alludes, I understand that the immediate relative is a father who is in very comfortable circumstances, and no application for a pension has been made.
I was speaking generally. I only mentioned that case as one coming under my own notice and quite near my own home.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I quite concur in the spirit of the hon. gentleman's observations.
Royal Northwest Mounted Police-Pensions to families of members of the force who lost their lives while on duty: Beatrice Maud and Laura May Grundy, $36.61; Margaret Johnson Brooke, $273.75; Annie Eva Emily and Arthur Stewart Mountford Brooke, $109.50 ; Mrs. Elizabeth Willmett, $54.75 ; Mrs. Elizabeth Fitzgerald, $525 ; pension to J. B. Allan, $450.
These seem to be very small pensions.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
In the case of Beatrice Maud and Laura May Grundy, the mother
has remarried, and the pension, as reduced, continues to the children.
Is the vote for Margaret lohnson Brooke a pension to a widow?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes, the widow of a sergeant who was drowned while on duty.

It does seem to me that $273.75 a year is a very small pension for a woman in the prairie west, especially for the wife of a sergeant. If this sergeant lost his life in the discharge of his duty I think the country could well afford to pay a larger pension.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: This is the same amount that has been voted for a number of years. In this case we do propose a supplementary estimate, for the reason that Mrs. Brooke has become insane, and there are circumstances, which I will explain on the Supplementary Estimates, which make it reasonable to make further provision.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: These pensions seem small, but they were recommended iby a board whose recommendation was confirmed by Parliament. The pensions were thought to be the best that could be done at that time. These oases are of old standing.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: They were all fixed after recommendation by the board.

Civil Government-Office of the Conservation Commission, $35,800.

Some information was
asked in regard to the Conservation Commission, and I had a memorandum prepared on the point which is as follows:
The work can be conveniently considered under the various branches of work:
(1)	Forests :
The Trent watersheds survey report is now in the press. This area was selected because it is typical of thousands of square miles of cut-over lands in eastern Canada, and because the $10,000,000 invested in the Trent waterway gives the Dominion Government a special interest in this region. The report contains valuable recommendations respecting the reforesting of this area and data respecting the possible returns from it, if reforested.
The railway fire protection work is now organized in the West, and, so far as possible, in the East. The tremendous decrease in fire damage and the cordial co-operation of the railway companies demonstrate the wisdom and economic results of the railway fire legislation.
Material progress in collecting statistics of our forest resources has been made in British Columbia and Saskatchewan. Much attention has been given to forest conditions on Dominion lands, particularly as regards disposal of waste in cutting and to natural reproduction through control of methods of cutting.
(2)	Fur-bearing animals:
A report on fur farming was published in 1913 and has already gone through two editions. Requests for it have been received from the principal European countries, Australia and the United States and Alaska. An enlarged and revised edition wdll be published in 1914. In Prince Edward Island there are 171 foxfarming companies with a capitalization of sixteen and oner-quarter millions.
(3 ) Fisheries:
A report of the Canadian oyster by Dr. Jos. Stafford was published in 1913. The total cost of the report to the commission other than the printing and binding, was a small honorarium to the author, the cost of the field investigations having been borne by the Department of Marine and Fisheries.
As a result of the interest excited by the Sea Fisheries report, published by the commission in 1912, the Government of British Columbia, in 1913, engaged Dr. Stafford to report on the transplanting of Atlantic oysters to the Pacific coast. The increasing interest in ovster-l'arming in the Maritime provinces, particularly Prince Edward Island, demonstrates the economic development of this industry.
(4)	Agriculture:
The agricultural surveys were continued in 1913. They are carried on to ascertain whether agriculture is improving or the reverse, whether weeds, insect pests, etc., were increasing or decreasing. Thirty illustration farms-not

experimental farms iii any sense of the word-were carried on at a cos't of less than $100 per farm They are designed to demonstrate that any farmer who will follow the recommendations of the agriculturists of the commission can obtain increased crops, can rid his farm of weeds and can increase its fertility. Farmers' improvement associations have been formed near each illustration farm and numerous addresses given by the agriculturists.
(5)	Public health:
Special attention has been given to the pollution of waters used for civic water supplies. Evidence has been presented to the International Joint Commission respecting a sanitary survey of international waterways, and to the Pollution of Streams Committee.
The collection and disposal of garbage in urban municipalities and sewage disposal have received attention. Town planning and housing have been studied and, next June, the commission will act as hosts to the National City Planning Conference in Toronto. This convention is exciting interest throughout Canada and it is hoped that it will result in the passage of enabling legislation along the lines suited to Canadian conditions.
(6)	Water-powers :
During 1913, the report on the proposition to dam the St. Lawrence at the Long Sault was published.
It contains in systematized form full information respecting Canada's rights on that river.
The water-powers of the Nelson. Hayes, Berens and Dauphin rivers in Manitoba were gauged, and in 1914 the work of the last three years will now be published as a report on the water-powers of the prairie provinces.
Work was continued on the water-powers of northern British Columbia. In 1914, the investigations of 1912, 1913 and 1914, covering the portion of the province lying between the Grand Trunk Pacific and the international boundary, will be published as a report on water-powers in British Columbia. A report of the waterworks and sewage systems of the Dominion was published in 1913.
(7)	Coal:
The conservation of coal report is now in the press. It advocates more economic methods of utilization, such as briquetting and use of byproduct coke ovens, and emphasizes the advantages of the leasehold system. The programme of work during the 1914 has not been finally decided upon, but wall deal, in general, with the power situation in Canada, utilization of lignite to develop power at central plants, &c.
The bulletin ' Conservation ' is issued monthly to all newspapers in Canada and to individuals who take an interest in the conservation of our natural resources.
The duty of the commission is to investigate, inquire, advise and inform. In so doing, they avoid, whenever possible, doing work that can be regarded as falling within the function of a governmental department. If it is occasionally necessary to do such work, it is only carried far enough to arouse interest in the work, or to indicate possible improvement, or to obtain the information necessary for intelligent judgment.
I was also asked for information as to the staff of the commission. Following is a list of the permanent officers and clerks

on the staff, together witn their official titles and salaries:
James White, assistant to chairman, salary, $5,000 ; Clyde Leavitt, chief forester, $2,800; Leo. G. Denis, hydro-electrical engineer, $2,400; Wm. J. Dick, mining engineer, $2,400; F. C. Nunnick, agriculturist, $2,300; Thos. Grindlay, draughtsman, $1,800; Allen Donnell, assistant editor, $1,650 ; Helen A. Grange, librarian, $750 ; Lucy Hawkins, clerk, $650 ; Nellie Pepper, clerk, $600 ; Lorna Burwash, clerk, $600 ; Nauma F. Johnson, clerk, $600 ; Alice Beaulieu, clerk, $550; J. A. Macdonald, clerk, $800; Kathleen McElroy, clerk, $550 ; James Carrol, messenger, $550 ; W. J. O'Connor, messenger, $500.
Mr. OLIVER; I notice that mention is made of a considerable amount of practical work done by the commission, particularly in agriculture and in water power investigation. I was under the impression that when the commission was organized it was intended to be educative and not administrative. It would appear to me, from the list of its activities which has been read, that the commission has, to a considerable extent, become administrative. There is no objection to that so long as the -vfrork is necessary and is well done, and so long as that work does not cover ground occupied by any of the departments. It may be said -and it is absolutely true-that there is room for all the work that can be done by the commission and any one of the departments in many of these lines, but it is surely much better to have a single than a divided responsibility. If we are to look to the Department of Agriculture for agricultural demonstration and education, then the activities of the Conservation Commission in that line are not required. There is, to some extent', a waste of money, and there is what strikes me as being much worse than the mere expense-the fact that the Agricultural Department, may as well as the Conservation Commission, fail to take notice of matters that they would otherwise deal with, the Department of Agriculture assuming that the Conservation Commission will deal with it, and the Conservation Commission assuming that the Department of Agriculture will take it up. It may be that there is a well-defined sharing of responsibility and consequently no overlapping or omissions, but so far as we are informed there has been no such arrangement. If not, either the Conservation Commission should confine itself to purely educative work, or else, if it is going into administrative work, the measure of its administrative responsibility should be thoroughly understood and lefined, as it is not likely to be by a general vote covering the total expenses in one sum.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I appreciate the importance of what my hon. friend has put before the committee. I may observe that the report which I have just read states that there is a desire and intention on the part of the commission not to duplicate the work of any department, and that in case they undertake any work which might seem to be the work of a department rather than that of the commission, they do so only for the purpose and to the extent of arousing interest in the subject. That is the intention they have; my hon. friend may have some doubt as to whether they give full effect to that intention. I know that the question of duplicating work is a very important one, and I entirely agree with what my hon. friend has said in that regard, but even among the departments of the Government, as he knows, there is sometimes a good deal of difficulty in avoiding some duplication. As between the commission and the several departments, I shall certainly use any influence I have to avoid duplication of the character alluded to by my hon. friend.
Mr. OLIVER; I said there were two points, of which the duplication was the minor point. The major point is the blank that may occur between the responsibilities assumed by the Conservation Commission and those assumed by the department. There may be, on the one hand, a duplication of over-lapping of work, and on the other hand-which is, to my mind, even more serious-a condition under which each party leaves the responsibility to the other, the result being that what should be done is not done.
.Mr. BORDEN: From the report which I have read, it would seem that the commission endeavours to exercise a certain amount of vigilance with regard to matters which, although properly coming within the activities of the various departments of Government, nevertheless have some relation to the work which the commission is supposed to carry on. If the commission observes that some such work or some particular phase of any work is not receiving the attention which, in the opinion of the commission, it should receive from the department, then the commission, for the purpose of arousing interest, undertakes some work of that kind. If that is a correct statement of conditions, it *would not be very likely that the difficulty to which my hon. friend has alluded would arise. I shall bear his observations in mind and if

he can suggest anything that might be done to avoid the detriment to the public interest which he regards as possible I would be very glad indeed to have the benefit of his suggestions or observations.

There is a matter
which I fancy is not irrelevant to this item, biit which L wish to draw to the attention of the right hon. Prime Minister. There are in this country landmarks and national monuments which we wish to preserve. I notice, in looking through the London Times, that the Board of Works in the old country have the right to prevent the sale or demolition of property or houses, by issuing an order so as to give the Board of Works a period of eighteen months in which they may purchase the property on behalf of the Government if they so decide. I do not know if there is a department in this Government which has that power or whether it would be wise for the Government to acquire such power. I should think it would, and as we are dealing with the question of conservation, perhaps not in a sense intended when the commission was formed, I make the suggestion that perhaps the Prime Minister might think it well to give the Conservation Commission the power to obtain such an order and later on, if Parliament so thought, acquire the property for national purposes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The question to which
my hon. friend has called my attention hardly seems to pertain to the scope Jof this commission; nevertheless, it is deserving of very serious consideration. The same question has been under the consideration of the Government. The hon. gentleman will remember that a commission was formed for the purpose of preserving and beautifying the battlefields in the vicinity of the city of Quebec. Representations have been made to the Government from various parts of the country pointing out the importance of acquiring and preserving monuments or building or places of especial historic interest. That subject has been under the consideration of the Minister of Finance and one or two other members of the Government, but at the present moment I have nothing to announce except that it is under consideration, and that we may possibly be able to make an anouncement in regard to this at a later date.

I am glad to hear the
declaration made by the right hon. gen-

tleman. We should do for our old fortifications and historic buildings what we have done for the Archives. For instance, it is well known that Dr. Doughty, a very able archivist, has practically authority to purchase any document of value to Canada; as a matter of fact, we know that for the last five or six years he has succeeded in getting from various countries, especially England, France and the United States, and I think even Russia, some most valuable documents for Canada. It seems to me that the Government should preserve historic fortifications. My hon. friend has referred to the Quebec Battlefields Commission. Everybody to-day acknowledges that no money could be better spent than in beautifying the surroundings of Quebec, and maintaining the landmarks around the battlefield. A commission, under the chairmanship of Sir George Garneau, has performed some very excellent work, and for my part I would not begrudge any sums of money that would be spent for like purposes.
The Art Commission appointed by the Government has also done some excellent work last year. Not very long ago I had occasion to visit the museum in Ottawa and I found that some very valuable paintings and sculptures, which are a credit to our country, had been purchased by the Government. The museum is now open to the public on Sundays, and this experiment has been such a success that it should induce the Government to also open the Archives on Sunday, and to enlarge the Archives building. Everybody knows that the building is already too small for its purpose, and I hope to see this year a vote for the enlargement of that very important building.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I appreciate the observations and suggestions of my hon. friend. It is very important that we should preserve, as far as possible, these objects of historic interest. The subject is under consideration. The Archives building will undoubtedly require enlargement in the near future. The subject has been brought to my attention by Mr. Doughty and I have already placed a communication before the Minister of Public Works about it.

Did the right hon. gentleman impress on my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works the idea that if the building is enlarged space should be provided for the Royal Society of Canada ? The members of the Royal Society meet here generally once a year, sometimes more

frequently, and they have no accommodation. The members are obliged to hold their sittings either at the Carnegie library or at the Normal school. It is not proper that this state society should hold its meetings outside of a public building belonging to the Government. As they also have a library and collections, etc., it seems to me that it would be proper for the Minister of Public Works to make provision in the Archives building for the accommodation of this society. It would be the most convenient place for the meeting of the members of this society.

Hon. GEO. P. GRAHAM: Shortly after the formation of the Conservation Commission; in connection with the investigation of other water-powers throughout Canada they looked ipto the water-powers that were created on the canals, such as the Lachine canal and the Welland canal. speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I imagine that the report in question would -appertain to the Department of Railways and Canals rather than to the commission, and the Minister of Railways can give my hon. friend more information on that than I can. I could not give my hon. friend any reliable information as to the number of cases in which that has been done, but I do know that several cases of very long standing have been disposed of within t'he past twelve months. If my hon. friend desires, I -will ask the Minister of Railways to prepare information on the subject.

The hon. gentleman
could hand me a synopsis of what has been done. There are quite a number of these leases, and as the new Welland canal is being constructed possibly some of the old rights will be interfered with in the new construction, and it 's interesting to know wlat has been -done. The Conservation Commission asked if they -might be allowed to -send their officer to investigate in the department, and I think he was given a free hand, but I have never been able to find out the result of his investigation.
