During the year, the question has come up whether it would not be in the interest of the Printing Bureau to have an Assistant King's Printer appointed, but we had no money, and so the appointment was not made.

My hon. friend says that some time during the year the question arose of appointing an Assistant King's Printer. That question is always present, as is the question of appointing men in every other department. But, he has not pointed out the reasons why this appointment should be made. The statute provides for four positions-King's Printer, Superintendent of Stationery, Superintendent of Printing and Accountant, and the occupant of each of these positions must, according to the Act, possess certain qualifications. In the past it has always been the custom to have the Superintendent of Printing replace the King's Printer when the King's Printer was absent through illness or other cause, because the King's Printer and the Superintendent of Printing are usually men of the same class of knowledge and technical ability. My hon. friend proposes now to change that by creating a new position which is not provided for under the statute, and for the creation of which, I venture to submit, he has not advanced any sufficient reason. The situation would probably be better understood if he would explain to the committee what duties the Assistant King's Printer would perform if appointed.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
First of all, I must say that the appointment of an Assistant King's Printer is quite authorized by the law. The hon. gentleman is right in saying that there are four positions specifically provided by the law, and which he has mentioned, hut there is in the law also a general clause authorizing the Governor in Council to appoint any other officers deemed necessary for the welfare of the department. During the illness of the late King's Printer, which lasted about six months, I believe, it was deemed desirable to have an assistant King's Printer to per-

form the duties which the law attaches to the King's Printer, but the appointment was not made, because unhappily the King's Printer died a few weeks ago. Other occasions might arise in the future making it necessary for the welfare of the Printing Bureau to appoint an assistant. The Superintendent of Printing, of course, is a good man and a faithful servant, but we find that in every department there is an assistant deputy minister, and I do not think there is any good reason why the same provision should not be made in the Printing Bureau. The hon. gentleman knows that there are between twelve and fifteen hundred men employed there.
No, I do not know that.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Then, I give the hon. gentleman that information. There are over twelve hundred men and women employed in the Printing Bureau to-day. That branch of the Administration is doing a large business, as the hon. gentleman knows, and I do not believe that any good reason can be given why, as it has been found necessary to have assistant deputy ministers in the other departments, it should not be desirable to have one in the Printing Bureau. This would not be the creation of a new position, because, under the very law passed in 1906, under which the King's Printer was appointed, Mr. McMahon, superintendent of printing, was appointed Assistant King's Printer. I assume that the reason was that an assistant to the deputy minister was found as necessary in this as in any other department.

My hon. friend has
completely proved my contention by citing the case he mentions. Mr. McMahon, in the absence of the King's Printer, was appointed Assistant King's Printer. But that did not involve the creation of a new position or an increase in the salary list. The Superintendent of Printing is supposed to possess the knowledge which will enable him to fill the position of King's Printer in that officer's absence. Under the law no special provision is made for the creation of the position of Assistant King's Printer, nor has provision been made for the salary by vote of this House. The hon. minister has not answered my question. I asked, . in the event of this position being created, and filled, what are to be the duties of the Assistant King's Printer as distinct from those allotted to the King's Printer [DOT]and the Superintendent of Printing?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: We must make a distinction between the case of the King's Printer being there at his work and the case of the King's Printer being compelled to be absent. Of course, in his absence the duties allotted to him will be performed by his assistant. But, even with the King's Printer attending to his duties, I submit, the task of controlling that branch of the Administration is too heavy for one man, however capable and competent he may be. The task should be shared with somebody else.
Does the hon. gentleman mean the printing branch?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: 1 mean the whole thing,, because the King's Printer has control of this whole department.
At that rate, the Assistant King's Printer will have control not only over the printing branch, but also over the stationery branch.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Yes, he will have to act in everything controlled by the King's Printer, under the King's Printer's orders.

If my hon. friend's contentions were well founded, he would have to have an assistant superintendent of stationery as well. He must know the provision of the Act whereby two superintendents are created, one for the printing branch and one for the stationery branch, relieving the King's Printer of the work to which he refers. There is no more reason for appointing an Assistant King's Printer who would look after the printing branch, than there would be to appoint an assistant superintendent of stationery, and very few possess the technical knowledge to look after both branches; in fact, I do not think there are any such men. But if he appoints one, he will find-even if it has not already been urged upon him-that demands will be made for the appointment of an assistant in the stationery branch.
What, then, would be that assistant's rank? Would he rank higher than the Controller of Stationery? The demands made upon my hon. friend were made upon every one of his predecessors, none of whom, however, yielded to them, knowing perfectly well that the department could be run properly with one responsible head, aided by two superintendents. I submit that my hon. friend has not given the committee any reason why this new position should be created. I sympathize very sincerely with him in the demands that I know are made

upon him for the creation of this position, but I say that he should not yield to them. If the position has been created and filled, I can only say that in my judgment it is simply a waste of public money to create a position for some gentleman whose friends have been clamorous enough to succeed in inducing the hon. gentleman, for whom I have the greatest respect, to do something that none of his predecessors would do.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I am in a position to say that no such demands have been made, so far as this position is concerned. I was the first who thought of it, and I thought of it after the two or three months had elapsed during which the King's Printer was unable to come to his office.
Who was looking after the Bureau during his absence?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The Superintendent of Printing was. the acting King's Printer. Before these Estimates were presented, no one but myself and the officials of the department knew there was such an item in the Estimates. Some time before the death of the King's Printer, I thought such an appointment should be made, but we had no money, and that is why an appointment has not been made. In the future the same circumstances might arise, *and I believe that in the interests of the -department we should have the money ready to pay any man who might be thought fit to fill that position. This vote does not mean that the appointment will be made, but in the case of such a necessity arising we would like to have the money to pay the man who might be appointed. I do not know whether or not I understood my hon. friend correctly, but I may say that there is no intention of appointing an assistant to the Superintendent of Printing or the Controller of Stationery:
There is just as much reason for appointing one as the other.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada

speechtext: Having some intimate knowledge of my hon. friend's office, I would be the last person in the House to object to the creation of this position, or even to criticise it, if the hon. gentleman advanced any reason why it should be created. In the same breath my hon. friend refutes himself; he says this position is badly needed, and at the same time he says it is not going to be filled.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Was badly needed.

It must be more badly
needed now, when there is no King's Printer.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
We expect to have one
soon.
Has he been appointed yet?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: No.

Judging from the observations of my l}on. friend, I should think that he intends to make the position of King's Printer a sinecure, and then have the assistants do the work. That will not contribute to the well-being of the institution. This Assistant King's Printer, according to my hon. friend, is to have authority over the stationery branch, that
is,	over the Superintendent of Stationery as well as over the Superintendent of Printing. My hon. friend says he did not hear anything about the appointment of an Assistant King's Printer. I take that cum grano salis, because several times during the past year the newspapers announced the appointment of an Assistant King's Printer, even mentioning the name of the gentleman who was to be appointed. This question of the appointment of an Assistant King's Printer has been rife for years, and I venture to say that every person who has occupied the position which I am glad to see my hon. friend filling has had that pressed on him from time to time. Heretofore those who pressed for the appointment were never able to satisfy the minister that there was any necessity for
it.	It is all very well for my hon. friend to say that the money will be voted and that the position will only be filled in case of an emergency: We understood the

day of emergency had passed; even this emergency at the Printing Bureau. Is it a fact that my hon. friend has leased premises outside the Printing Bureau, to which he has transferred the Stationery Branch?
Mr. CODERRE-. Yes.

Then there is all the less reason why he should appoint the Assistant King's Printer. In all kindness, I wish to tell my hon. friend that the leasing of such premises and the dividing of the institution was what led to mismanagement and waste and loss a few years ago. The remedy for the over-crowded state of the Printing Bureau is not the leasing of new premises or the appointment of an Assistant King's Printer, but the building of a new Printing Bureau with ample accommodation for both branches. I presume my hon. friend has been obliged to seek premises elsewhere for the purpose of accommodating the stock of supplies and giving those employed in the Stationery Branch a chance to fill the orders from the different departments and from the Houses of Parliament. But that removes a large body of officials, some of whom occupy very responsible positions, from the Printing Bureau proper, and from under the eye of the official who, under the Act, is responsible to the minister and to Parliament for the proper conduct of both branches of the Department of Public Printing and Stationery.
I would urge my hon. friend to secure a site at the very earliest date and proceed with the erection of a Printing Bureau which would be ample for the needs of the Government for the next fifty years. This division of labour, of stock and of supplies is one of the worst things that can be done. It was owing to it that great losses took place in years past. It is impossible to properly carry on an institution if it is divided in this way. There can be no proper check on deliveries or outgoings and in the end there will be loss, dissatisfaction, and endless trouble for the hon. gentleman or his successor. I again urge that neither the appointing of an Assistant King's Printer nor the leasing of new premises in different parts of the city will constitute a remedy for existing troubles. The remedy lies in the erection of a new building.

I understand that the
selection of the new King's Printer has not yet been made by the Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: No.

I suppose he has many applications and the names I see in the papers are all excellent names. I have seen especially the name of Mr. de la Broquerie Tache who is a gentleman from our province and well fitted for that position. Mr. Tache, although he is a political opponent of mine, is certainly well able to fill that post. He has been connected with the press and with printing establishments for over twenty-five years. He belongs to a highly respectable family, and I think he deserves well from the Government. If the choice should be that of Mr. Tache it would meet with the approval of the entire province.
I would like to say a word about another appointment, to fill the position, of the late assistant archivist, Mr. Roy. Last year I understood the Postmaster General to say that the best appointment would be made. When the question of appointing an archivist came before the last Cabinet, political qualification were not thought of. Dr. Doughty was appointed, he w'as a newcomer in the country but he was taken because of his special fitness for the office and his appointment has certainly been a credit to Canada. Then came the appointment of Mr. Edmond Roy, of Quebec, as assistant archivist. Certainly, as regards French archives, he was an authority, not only in Canada but in France. Mr. Roy was a well-known Conservative, but Mr. Fisher, who was then Minister of Agriculture, did not care about his politics; he appointed Mr. Roy on account of his special qualifications, and I am bound to say that that appointment was hailed with pleasure by all those who took especial interest in the archives. If an appointment has not been made to the position of assistant, I would urge upon my hon. friend that he should select the man who is best equipped for that very special post. I have no recommendations to make except, perhaps, the one I have made verbally to my hon. friend. I think I suggested the name of Mr. Massicotte, now in the court house in Montreal, who, I think, is one of the electors of the Secretary of State. The hon. member knows that he is well versed in all matters pertaining to archives and history in general.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I am obliged to say to the hon. member for Rouville that Mr. Fabien Vanasse has been appointed to fill that vacancy.
When ?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
About a month or six weeks ago. Of course I believe that the

Government will have to appoint a King's Printer pretty soon. Several names have been mentioned in the press and elsewhere, and I believe that all these names will meet the same approval from my hon. friend, because they are names of persons who are capable of filling the position very well. I believe I should be thankful to the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Murphy), who has had experience and who has given me to-night the benefit of that experience. I have read the reports made by the commissions who investigated the whole situation in the Printing Bureau. Both reports advise that a new building should be erected as soon as possible. The necessary money for the completion of plans will be found not in these Estimates but in the Supplementaries for this year. The question of finding a site has been considered but not completely settled yet. I really believe it should be settled as soon as possible, so that we may be able to bring under the same roof all the branches of the Printing Bureau. Lately we have been obliged to rent another building situated at the corner of Dalhousie and York streets. There were several reasons for that. One reason is that there is not sufficient space for the officers and employees of the Bureau, and another is that lately, according to a report made by the chief architect of the Public Works Department, that building was in a dangerous condition, being overloaded. The danger was imminent, and upon that report the Minister of Public Works has rented another building in which today the stationery branch is housed. There is no division. The King's Printer will still have charge over the whole work. This sum of $4,000 was placed in the Estimates during the illness of the late Mr. Parmelee to pay for an assistant, as the need was very great. We will have a King's Printer soon, tout I do not want to be understood as stating that the Assistant King's Printer will be appointed immediately after the vote is passed; I believe it would be in the interests of the Printing Bureau to have this vote put through in case similar circumstances arise again, and for that reason I would ask my hon. friend to withdraw his opposition to this item.
Mr. MURPHY; Will my hon. friend tell us what the duties of the Assistant King's Printer will be, when the King's Printer himself is attending to his duties?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
The Printing Bureau
seems to be a place to which the working

class in the city of Ottawa go to find employment. They have always gone there, and I suppose they always will. I have been to the Bureau several times, and on each occasion I have found several men waiting to see the King's Printer, with a view to getting work. It is not according to law that these people should (bother the life out of the King's Printer to get employment, but he has to receive them and try to give them work, and when he is so employed, it is impossible for him to supervise the work of the whole Bureau.
Even ministers have that trouble.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
If the appointment of
an assistant would relieve the King's Printer of these callers, I would suggest that the appointment be made to-day.
It is a labour bureau you want to establish.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: We all know it is a labour bureau, and it cannot be otherwise. The King's Printer has to see these men and 'he cannot do that without neglecting more important duties. Somebody else should be there to help him.

Perhaps my hon. friend will not mind my giving him a bit of advice, not that I suppose it will be taken. You never can tell when you sow seed, what fruit it will bring forth. I have had some experience in the printing business, and so far as the qualifications are concerned, I believe I could help sfelect a man for that job. The Act specifies that he must be a publisher or printer who hac been actively engaged, as such, for ten years, but it is a mistake to think that even the auost fluent writer in the world would necessarily be fitted for that position.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: Would you qualify under the Act?
I have had the experience, I do not say anything ahou! the further qualifications.

If the hon. gentleman
(Mr. Graham) does, will you appoint him?

A man is not necessarily qualified for that position just because he is editor of a paper. The meaning of the statute is, a man who has had practical experience as a printer or as a practical publisher.
That is what Mr. Taohe is.

To my mind, this large
department which is the printing establishment for the Government ought, to have a man with great executive ability. He should be able to organize the men under him; not that he should be labouring so earnestly himself in small matters, because the test of a good organizer is not that he works himself to death but that he gets the men under him to do the work. If this man has not good executive ability, he will make a mess of the Printing Bureau. A large number of men are employed there, and it takes considerable skill to run an establishment of that size with the minimum of friction and the maximum of good results. After executive ability, and outside the statutory qualifications, the King's Printer .should be a man who is in touch with the printing business so that he could go to ithe Bureau, and on looking it over, see whether the work was being done properly. He should be able to look over the heads of his subordinates occasionally and discover any possible leaks. What I want to impress on my hon. friend is that it is a mistake to think that because a man is a good newspaperman he is well qualified for this position. He ought to be an organizer of men, of great executive ability, and one who can handle men, if yon will allow me to put it roughly. That he should have some knowledge of printing and publishing is required by the statute. If my hon. friend would get a .man with the qualifications I have outlined, it will not matter much whether he can write an article or not. While that would be an advantage it is not necessary, and a man might have that qualification and not be fit for this position at all.

I would like to ask my hon. friend why so much printing is being done outside the Bureau. Is it because the staff of the bureau is insufficient,
9 p.m. or simply to give some pap to the Conservative newspapers?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
The reason was given
by the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Murphy) a few minutes ago. It is because the building is too small. My hon. friend can rest assured that we could find sufficient employees, but we have not got room for them. The men are cramped as it is. I know that under the late regime, the hon. member for Russell intended to put a certain sum in the Estimates to buy a site.
It was in the Estimates.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The reasons why a new building should be erected then may be stronger to-day. With a new building sufficiently large it will be possible for the department to do all the necessary printing. This was the object of the Act.

It is astonishing when we go through the Auditor Genreal's report, to see how much money is paid to outside printers. I will mention a few of the largest of these items. I commence with an item which I have no doubt will be interesting to the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers). The Winnipeg Telegram received $15,365.16 for printing and $4,972.75 for advertising; Toronto World, $9,067.40 for advertising; Southam Press, $19,005.35; News, $10,165.89 for advertising; Mail and Empire, $12,641.71. Even the Orange Sentinel got over a thousand dollars-$1,554.
How much did the Eye Opener get?

The Eye Opener of Calgary got $261.70. The St. John Standard, which is known to be the organ of the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen), received $13,415.33 for printing, and $2,717.76 for advertising; the Quebec Chronicle, the English Conservative newspaper of Quebec, got $5,330.92 for printing and $5,645.60 for advertising; L'Evenement, the organ of the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier), got $18,728.73 for printing.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: I have no organ.

But tl at is not all; besides that it received $4,644.78 for advertising; the Montreal Gazette got the lion's share-$24,903.55 for printing and $5,331.17 for advertising; and La Patrie got $18,110.37 for printing and $5,298 for advertising. I see here the Southam Press. It appears to be ubiquitous; we see it in Toronto, Montreal and Winnipeg. The Southam Press in Montreal got $12,788.39. The Ottawa Citizen got $6,678.53, and the Ottawa Journal, $3,835.70.
What did the Free Press get?

The Free Press got only $155.16. The Kingston Standard, another good Conservative newspaper, got $3,849.16 for printing, and $3,544.95 for advertising. The Lachute Watchman got $176.19. The hon. 'member for Argenteuil (Mr. Perley), was more reasonable and more moderate than the others. The London Free Press received $7,799.30; the Dawson News, $315

for printing and $3,711 for advertising, and the Halifax Herald got $9,812.52 for printing and $3,500.42 for advertising. I am told that the editor of this newspaper is a senator appointed .by this Government. The Hamilton Spectator, another good Conservative newspaper, got $4,785.04 for advertising and $180, for printing.
How much did the Hamilton Times get?
It did not receive one cent.
That is all right.

I suppose it was too Grit for this Government. Then the Fredericton Gleaner got $1,290.33 for advertising, and $932.02 for printing. The Charlottetown Examiner got $1,171.15 for advertising and $1,881.69 for printing. I am not going to mention them all because it would take too long. I must not forget the Brock-ville Times; it i. eeived $675.88, but I do not see the name of the newspaper of my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham). The Belleville Intelligencer got $1,571.75.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: How much did the papers in the county of Victoria, Nova Scotia, get?

They got free delivery
on a steamer within the last couple of weeks.

It is astonishing to see how much money is paid to outside printers. Certainly a large amount of this printing could be done at the Printing Bureau.
As far as the advertising is concerned, they advertise small contracts for $100, $150 or $200 in about a dozen newspapers. It is a pure waste of money. There should be a retrenchment in this department, and I hope the Secretary of State will stop the leakage.

Three or four years ago, the then Minister of Public Works was taken to task because no tenders were asked for the advertisements published in the press. Where is my hon. friend from Pee) (Mr. Blain)? Does he remember one evening. in this House when he declared war on the then Minister of Public Works because, forsooth, he had not called for tenders for advertisements? I would like to know what his opinion is about these advertisements being given now without any tenders. My hon. friend is consistent, and I am quite sure he does not like to admit to be good on

the part of his friends what he declared to be bad on the part of his opponents. Here are hundreds of thousands of dollars spent for advertisements in the Tory press without any tenders being called for. What does my hon. friend think of that? I will expect an answer from him.

Did the Secretary of
State say that plans were prepared for a new Printing Bureau ?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
No. The vote for the
plans Will be found in the supplementary Estimates for this year. As far as the buying of the site is concerned, the question has been brought up but no decision has been reached.

In conection with the
site I would suggest that my hon. friend induce his colleagues to follow the course they have so often followed before, in respect to that feature of their policy which is always evident wdien we criticise any of their actions, and when they retort: That is what you did. If they will in this case follow the course of their predecessors, we on this side of the House will have no criticism to offer. The site it was proposed to purchase was one which I mentioned before to this committee, I think when the hon Mr. Roche was Secretary of State. The site I mentioned was the old St. Lawrence and Ottawa depot, which is bounded north and isouth by Sussex and Dalhousie streets respectively, and east and west by Botelier street and Bingham square. It is a large block of land having the advantage of a railway track. It would fill every requirement of a large manufactory with regard to light and air, and would permit of any expansion that might be required within the next fifty years.
I was rather amazed to hear my hon. friend say that the number of employees of the Printing Bureau was now over 1,200. That being the case, I am not so much surprised that it was found necessary to move part of the outfit to other premises. The last time a return was brought down,
I think the number of employees was 750.
I can scarcely Gonceive that the business done by the Printing Bureau has increased to such an extent within a couple of years as to justify the employment of 1,200 people now. That is a matter, however, in regard to which we can get fuller information when my hon. friend's main Estimates are under discussion. I would impress

upon him the necessity of a new building and the immediate purchase of a site. While my hon. friend is not under any obligation to take the advice tendered by my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) or by myself, istill as a citizen who was born here and who has lived here all his life, I would like to impress upon my hon. friend that there is no better site in the city of Ottawa than the one I have mentioned.
It fills the requirements in this particular, that it will be close to the residences of most of the employees of the Printing Bureau who have located in that part of the city known as Lower Town.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
What about the site on
Wellington street?

I would not approve of that at all. I understand that my hon. friend proposes to erect some very handsome structures on Wellington street. The office portion of the Printing Bureau might be architecturally fine, but there would be a portion of it which would be similar to that of a manufacturing establishment; there would be a place for the boilers and the chimney, and there would be smoke and grime which are always associated with a manufacturing establishment. For these reasons I would not like to see it on any part of Wellington street. As regards the site I mentioned, the office portion of the building and the stores portion of the building could both be located on the side nearest to Sussex street, as that is the portion which people would see as they passed back and forth to Rockliffe or the east end of the city, while the manufacturing part of the building could be in the rear, down towards Dalhousie street and close to the tracks of the Canadian Pacific railway. That was the idea in mind when the site was spoken of and practically decided upon. When the present Government came into power there was an item of $100,000 in the Estimates as a preliminary amount to be expended in the purchase of a site.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
You would have to tear
down the present building.

Yes, the present building is an unsightly one and should be pulled down in view of the improvements to the park and Nepean Point. If this suggestion is carried out, both the Minister of Public Works and the Secretary of State will hear no objections from this side of the House.

Why the necessity of an Assistant King's Printer? What positions do the King's Printer and Assistant King's Printer occupy? I am perfectly willing to see every department properly manned. I am not afraid to spend money on necessary service, but I am opposed to unnecessary service in a Government department as much as in a private business. I see no necessity for having two King's Printers.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I gave these explanations to the House a few minutes ago, but I am willing to repeat them for the benefit of my hon. friend. This item of $4,000 is for the position of an Assistant King's Printer and was put in the Estimates a few weeks or a month before the death of the late King's Printer. Seeing that the King's Printer had been sick for about five or six months, I thought that in the interest of the Printing Bureau the appointment of an Assistant King's Printer was necessary, and I brought that proposition before the Governor in Council.
But there was no money to pay an Assistant Kings' Printer. As we were preparing these Estimates we put in this item of $4,000; and, though the King's Printer had died in the meantime, and though his successor will soon be appointed, I believe that this item should remain in case circumstances should arise making it necessary to fill this office of Assistant King's Printer. I have said that I believe the appointment of such an officer is absolutely necessary, because the King's Printer has more to do than ought to be put upon one man.
Did Mr. Parmelee apply for an assistant?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
No, but the hon. gentleman will remember that when Mr. Parmelee was appointed an assistant was given him in the person of Mr. McMahon, who was Superintendent of Printing, and I believe the present Superintendent of Printing was appointed at the same time.	Thus we had a
King's Printer, an Assistant King's Printer and a Superintendent of Printing. But then in 1908 the Printing Bureau was not nearly so large as it is now. In view of all the conditions, we believe it would be wise to provide the money in case the appointment of an Assistant King's Printer may be found necessary.
Will the hon. minister please state the value of the work done in the Printing Bureau ?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada

speechtext: How much is done outside?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I am not sure, but I think about $400,000.

Has the Government considered the policy of decentralizing that Bureau by establishing branches in diff-ferent parts of the country, and especially in the West? I am told that men who understand these matters consider it a waste of money to have the work centralized. Has any attention been given to this matter by the Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I have never heard it mentioned.	.

Are any changes proposed in regard to the printing of documents in French in the Bureau? In the past great difficulty has been experienced in relation to this matter, and even when the Estimates came up for consideration the other day they were not printed in French. I inquired into this matter some years ago, when I had the honour to be Speaker of this House. I was told that the rule of the Bureau was to do the English printing first and then go on with the French. Of course, the great majority of members of this House understand English, but the delay in printing documents in French is a great inconvenience to French-speaking members, newspapers and to the Frenchspeaking public generally.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Acting according to the wishes of the right hon. the Prime Minister, and, of course, according to my own wishes,
I have included in these Estimates, as hon. members will see, an amount which, if voted, will pay for the services of three French translators at the Bureau. The reports of the Department of Trade and Commerce, the Insurance Branch, and the Auditor General always appear too late in French. Under the advice of the Chief Translator of the House, Mr. Desaulniers, I have come to the conclusion that the reports can be translated at the Bureau. This, I believe, will help to solve the difficulty to which the hon. gentleman refers.
Do I understand that in the various departments there are translators?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I know that there are two translators in the Mines Division, Mr. Sauvalle and Mr. Paradis, also that there are translators in the Department of Marine and Fisheries and one in the Post Office Department. As to the other departments, I am not informed.

The hon. minister will
realize, of course, that to print documents late is to waste money. The printing in French should go on simultaneously with the printing in English. There has been an improvement in this matter within the last, two or three years, but further improvement is possible. The documents should be sent to the King's Printer in both languages and the printing in the two languages should be simultaneous. I hope the minister will consider that, because it is important that all our people should have opportunity to inform themselves on public affairs. The French members of this House send out many blue books and other documents, but if these are late in being issued in French, they are of little or no value. I trust the minister will signalize his coming into office by making a sound rule in this respect. It need not involve any larger expenditure, ahd it will mean that the expenditure made will be really useful instead of mere waste.

(Translation.) I wish to say a few words in French, and I am addressing myself more particularly to you, Mr. Chairman (Mr. Blondin).
I am concerned with the translation of the Votes and Proceedings of this House. I do not know whose translation that is, but, really, it is very bad. I have before me No. 19 of the Votes and Proceedings, and I have checked off with the pencil at least one hundred and fifty barbarisms, anglicismis, I was going to say stupid blunders.
I shall stop at that. Instead of handing over that copy to the Speaker, it is preferable, I think, that I should let you have it, Mr. Deputy Speaker. I am aware that you have taken a keen interest in the appointment of a new staff of translators, and we approved of that wise departure; but it is only fair to insist that such translators shall be competent.
I shall appeal to the hon. Postmaster General, to the Secretary of State and to the Deputy Speaker of the House. . . .
(Translation.) Is that translation made by the translators of ' Hansard? '

(Translation.) I cannot say, but I do not think it is. I believe it is done by the translators of the House of

Commons. ' Hansard/ that is the official report of the debates of the House, is translated by a special staff of translators, while the translation of the Votes and Proceedings of the House of Commons is made by translators appointed by the Speaker and by the Committee of Internal Economy of this House.
I shall now, Sir, hand over No. 19 of the Votes and Proceedings, and you will agree with me that, if we are to pay salaries to the translators appointed by you, we have the right to expect them to turn out a fairly good translation.

(Translation.) Mr. Ohair-. man, is the translation of the Votes and Proceedings the work of men appointed by you?
Hon. L. P. PELLETIER (Translation.) The translation to which the bon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) has referred just now, is not the work of the translators appointed during recess. From . information just supplied to me, the translation referred to is the work of men who have been long in the service of this House, and concerning whose ability no doubt has heretofore been expressed. However, on looking over this copy of the Votes and Proceedings, as I have just done, I must admit that my hon. friend has certainly some grounds for complaint. It may be that the officer responsible for this work has not been in a position to supervise and control the work as he should have done. The hon. member may rest assured that I shall go into the matter to-morrow morning at the latest, and find out what are the facts.
However, I wish to point out that this translation is not the work of the translators recently appointed. They are entrusted with translation which formerly was being turned out much less speedily, as it was parcelled out to people living in various parts of the Dominion. To-day that translation is not given out to outsiders; it is all done in one and the same office. That has put a stop to one of the causes of delay of which the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Mareil) complained a moment ago. There is a great improvement, due to the fact that to-day we have those translators within our reach and on the spot.
As I stated a moment ago, the grievance voiced by the hon. member for Rouville appears to me at first sight to be well grounded, and he may be .sure that not later than to-morrow morning I shall see to it that ' there is no recurrence of similar facts.
Have the rates for advertising been increased since the Government came into power?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I cannot say positively, but I do not think so. So far as I am concerned, there has been no increase whatever.

There used to be one
rate applicable to printing in all that portion of the country east of Port Arthur, and an increased rate for printing done west of Port Arthur. Have these rates been changed?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: They have not.

Has my hon. friend
taken any action with regard to the appointment of Mr. Vanasse as assistant to the Dominion Archivist, Dr. Doughty?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Yes; he has been recommended by the Civil Service Commission.

As my hon. friend
knows, this position requires very special qualifications. Has the appointment of Mr. Vanasse been approved by Dr. Doughty?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I have known Mr. Vanasse for a number of years; I know that he is a good writer and has always been fond of historical research, particularly in Canadian history. I must confess that his name was not mentioned to me by Dr. Doughty. I mentioned his name to Dr. Doughty, who happened to know him well; and he declared that he would be well satisfied if Mr. Vanasse got the position.
The moment Dr. Doughty is satisfied I am. I have no doubt Mr. Vanasse will make a good assistant, but I wanted to know whether he had been recommended by Dr. Doughty.

Are tenders called for
printing done outside the Printing Bureau?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
No, not generally.
Tenders are asked in some cases, but as a rule the work is.paid for according to what are called Bureau rates.

If there is advertising
to be done, who decides what newspapers will get it?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I do.
Have you a list of newspapers to which you give advertising?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: There was a list in the department when the Government came into power, but I must admit that it has been corrected.
What steps has one to take to get his name on that list?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Members of this House have written to me asking that this or that newspaper be added to the list, and I complied with the request in almost all cases.

Would you give an
advertisement to a Grit newspaper?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Certainly I would.
Thank you.
Are the rates for printing the same for large as for small contracts?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Yes. Except in those cases where tenders have been called the work is paid for according to the Bureau rate, which is so much a page whether the work is large or small.

In considering the construction of a new printing office, the greatest care should be taken to make proper provision for ventilation.
There are two or three things necessary in a printing office,- first, perfect light, because the printing business is perhaps the hardest on the eye. Unless you have perfect light, not only is it impossible to do the work but the eyes of the employees will soon give out. Good light is a prime necessity, and if I were Secretary of State I would insist that plans should be designed only after a visit to one of the biggest printing establishments on this continent to ascertain just the necessities of the case. If a building is rushed up that might do for an ordinary manufacturing establishment, and the printers, proof-readers, type-setters, and pressmen are asked to work there, the work will not be well performed, and it will be very hard on the employees. The second point is that of perfect ventilation. The difficulty with most of our Government buildings is that they have not proper ventilation.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Including this building.

I think there is no building excluded. In some of these offices when a deputation is heard the air gets so thick it is impossible to think, and everybody gets drowsy. Then you put up the window and wait until it clears out, but by that time the room is cold and some person may become seriously ill. In addition to that the fumes from the metal in the type-setting machines and the odours from the ink and several other things make it absolutely imperative, in a printing office more than in any other manufacturing institution, that

you should have perfect ventilation. The plans for an ordinary building for rough manufacturing will not do for a printing establishment.

May I supplement the
suggestion made by my hon. friend by telling the Secretary of State that the essentials which have been laid down by my hon. friend he will find carried out in the new Curtis Publishing Company's building in Philadelphia; in the Doubleday-Page Company's building, Garden City, Long Island, in a new building in Indiana, close to Chicago; and also in the more modern parts of the United States Printing Office at Washington. These several institutions I visited a few years ago when we were discussing the erection of a new Printing Bureau and the features to which the hon. member for South Renfrew has called attention were found to have been especially considered in the erection of these different buildings. Either an inspection should be made by my hon. friend of these buildings or he should send to inspect them the architect charged with the work, so that the result may be the duplication of some of these features in the new Printing Bureau in Ottawa, to the very great benefit of persons employed there and the more efficient production of the output of such an establishment.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I shall certainly take a note of the remarks made by the hon. gentlemen on these points and will suggest that the architect visit those large establishments before plans are made;

Would my hon. friend inform this House whether all the typos and printers at the Bureau are union men and how many French-speaking typos are employed in the Printing Bureau, and how many English speaking ? Is the work done indiscriminately by English and French typos? Is not the lesser number of French typos the cause of the delay in the distribution of French blue-books?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I do not believe all of the men employed there belong to the labour union, but most of them do. They are paid according to the law applying to the Government Printing Bureau. Those rates are the rates obtaining in Montreal and Toronto. An agreement has been made between the employers in Toronto and Montreal, and the union, and we are obliged to follow that to a certain extent. On that point I believe the men are pretty well satisfied. I have been obliged lately

to give them a small increase in salary, but only on being satisfied that the salary paid here was lower than that paid the same class of workmen in Toronto and Montreal. I could not tell exactly the number of French and English typos.
The same amount of work has to be done in French and English ?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
Therefore, every compositor should be able to set up type in either language ?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I believe that is what is done.

The only complaint I have is that all of the printing was done in English first before the French was taken up. Some arrangement could be made by which it would go out simultaneously in the two languages, and then there would be no dissatisfaction.	_

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: There was more than one reason for the delay, and one of the reasons was that the translation was too late. Now, as far as the reports of the debates of the House of Commons are concerned, I know the translation is made without delay. I was told by Mr. Desaul-niers that they are translating from the English copy in manuscript; they do not have to wait until a version of the report is printed. Another reason, and this is the one mentioned by the hon. member for Bonaventure, is that they do not work at the Bureau on the two languages simultaneously. I do not know whether this can be done now in the space at our disposal. Soon, I hope, we shall have another building, and then we shall be able to do it.

Seeing that both languages are official, I think it is very important that there should be a French section in the establishment. These documents have to be printed in both languages and that can only be done by having a French section of the Bureau, which could be turning out the French copy simultaneously with the English.

(Translation). What
are the working hours?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: (Translation). Forty-eight hours per week.

(Translation). Is it the
intention of the hon. minister to adopt the eight-hour day?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
(Translation):	It has
been adopted already.

May I add another word to what has already been said with reference to the publication of ' Hansard ' in French? The matter which has been brought up by my hon. friend from Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) was under consideration four years ago, when the present Judge Gervais, then member .for Montreal, was Chairman of the Debates Committee. Through him and his committee, a new arrangement was made in conjunction with the Printing Bureau by which ' Hansard ' was brought out in French much more quickly than it had previously been. Certain rules were drawn up and printed, and the Secretary of State will find a copy of those rules, possibly in his own department, certainly down at the Printing Bureau. At that time certain changes were made in the matter of translating, producing copy, having it sent to the Bureau and having the proofs read, to the end that the publications in French and English might be produced simultaneously,
10 p.m. and, if that was not possible, then to have the French copies issued as speedily as they could be produced. A very marked improvement was made at that time, and I have no doubt the process is carried out under the regime of my hon. friend. There are a great many reasons why this occasional delay occurs, but with co-operation between the branches of Parliament, and the departments, and the Printing Bureau, there is no good reason why there should be any substantial delay in connection with any of these publications. It simply entails constant attention to the details of the work and good will on the part of those charged with producing it. My hon. friend will find that, if these conditions exist, the French publications will come out almost at the same time as the English publications, as undoubtedly they should.

The change brought about by Mr. Gervais consisted chiefly in having the ' Hansard ' office send a duplicate copy to the Printing Bureau and the translators' office. The translation went on while the English version was being printed. The French copy was afterwards sent to the Bureau, where there were two proofreaders, and the result was that the French ' Hansard ' was delivered here 24 hours after the English ' Hansard.' The result was very satisfactory in every respect. I do not know whether the same arrangement still continues, but we are not complaining

about the French ' Hansard ' so much as the other reports.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Perhaps the committee would be interested in knowing what improvements the translators have brought about. I have before me a statement showing the translation done from July X, 1912, to January 27, 1913, practically six months. The total number of pages translated was 6,904. I have also a statement showing the work done by the new organization from September 16, 1913, to January 28, 1914. That is only four months as compared with the other six months, and in those four months the number of pages translated was 9,206.

Does that statement
show what reports and blue book have been translated?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Yes, it gives everything in detail. There is the report of the Committee on Agriculture and Colonization, the Veterinary Director General's Report; reports of the Railway Commission, Technical Education Commission, Naval Department, Postmaster General's Report, and so on. So that under the new regime 9,206 pages were translated in four months, whilst under the old regime only 6,904 pages were translated in six months. That is a great improvement.

Do the translators still
complain about the Printing Bureau? The old complaint used to be that the copy was sent down there, and allowed to remain for weeks and sometimes months before being attended to. They placed the fault on the Printing Bureau. Has that been altered? Does the Printing Bureau proceed with the copy as soon as it gets it?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: We will make inquiries about that.

If the Printing Bureau
proceeded with the work as soon as they received the French copy, I do not think there would be any trouble.	.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: If the reports are wanted in both languages, I believe part of that work will have to be done outside.

As the Government has appointed additional translators and materially increased the translating staff, there is no reason why we should not aim at getting the reports in French and English simultaneously. It is a matter of right, and we have been bringing it up for years and years at every session but without results. I am quite ready to admit that the Government

took the right step when last year it increased the staff of translators, and now that a start has been made in this matter, why should we not complete it? The country expects that the blue books shall be distributed to the French section as well as to the English section of the community. They ought to be published simultaneously, and my hon. friend should see that they are, now that the copy gets in in due time. My hon. friend has been in journalism for a number of years, so have I, and so has my hon. friend from Bona-venture (Mr. Marcil) and we all know that a French blue book from Ottawa was a standing joke in the French editorial staffs. If a Freneh-Canadian journalist wanted to quote from a blue book, from the Auditor General's Report or from the report of the Postmaster General, or from any other report he had to wait at least twelve months before he could get it. That is not fair. As a result the people of our province were deprived of the benefit of the information contained in the blue books. The members could send a certain number to their constituents. The journalists had to translate from the blue books printed in English and, as a matter of fact, the press of the province of Quebec, and part of the press of the Maritime provinces, was deprived of the benefit of the information contained in the blue books. Now we have reorganized the translation office. I think we have appointed good men with the exception of those who translated this Journal of the House. Let us now complete that work and see that the blue books are published and distributed in French and English simultaneously. If the Secretary of State can accomplish that feat he will deserve well of his province.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I have already been
trying to do something in that line.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
My experience in my own department has been very much the same. I would like to put on the table of the House, as the law requires, the two versions of the report of my department at - the same time. We have been hammering at the Printing Bureau and trying to get the French version at the same time as the English version, but they say that they cannot do it; it is a matter of utter impossibility. They say: We have neither the space nor the men; if we had a Printing Bureau, such as that which has been very properly suggested by the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Murphy), we would be able to do the work, but it is out of the question

now; we cannot do it. I have been urging upon my colleague the Secretary of State that the report should he sent outside, but they have begun upon the work and it is too late to send it outside. There is not enough space and not enough men to get out the two versions at the same time. The suggestion made by my hon. friend from Rouville is a very proper one. If the Printing Bureau cannot do the work they should not undertake it. Let it be done outside and let us have it as we should have it.

I might refer to a report which was handled last year by the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Roche) on the question of immigration. The report was prepared by Mr. Asselin, a very interesting report, and, as my hon. friend knows, one that was well prepared. I have been asking for that report since last year but I have not been able to get it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: In French?

In French. It was prepared in French. It is a very important report and I would like to get it. I have always taken a deep interest in this question of immigration from France and Belgium, but up to the present time I have been unable to get the report. This report was sent in nearly two years ago, and yet we have only been able to get a typewritten copy. It is not fair to the members speaking the French language that we should have to wait so long for a report which is of special interest to our province.

I would like to remind the committee that the French version is as official as the English version. We always refer to the French translation of these documents, but we must not forget that the publication of a document in the French language is as official as it is in the English language. I might mention the unfortunate position in which I was placed two years ago upon my return from France. I had met certain public men there who were anxious to become familiar with the governmental affairs of Canada, and they asked me to send information upon the subject. I consulted the library and I was in many instances obliged to send over blue books printed in the English language because of the delay in the printing of the blue books in the French language. The French translators say: We have done our share, but the fault lies at the Printing Bureau. I hope that this difficulty will be overcome if we get a new Printing Bureau. Canada is going ahead by leaps and bounds, 47
our trade with France has increased to $15,000,000, our trade with European countries is rapidly increasing and I hope the Government will see to it that the French language is given its proper share of attention in the preparation of official publications.

I must say to the hon. Secretary of State that I believe it is necessary to appoint a King's printer who knows thoroughly both languages and can give fair play to both nationalities.
It is one of my reasons for insisting upon the .appointment of M. Tache, who is thoroughly able, and being well acquainted with the needs of the two official languages of this country, he would see to it that justice be done to both nationalities.

While my hon. friend the Secretary of State may have some sins to answer for, a good deal of the criticism that has been directed towards the delay in getting out the publications in French is really a matter that does not appertain to the Department of the Secretary of State. The Printing Bureau should be what its name indicates: it should not be any part of the business of the Printing Bureau to do translation. There should not be any translators there. The Printing Bureau should be supplied with copy ready for the printer without the intervention of any other class of people, just as copy is supplied to any other printing establishment. It is a mistake to mix the printing and the translation. The translation should be something apart from the Printing Bureau altogether. I only mention this because a good deal of discussion has centred upon the delay which I believe undoubtedly takes place in connection with the translation. This delay, I am bound to say in all fairness, is not the fault of my hon. friend or of the officials who are employed under him at the Printing Bureau and who should be called upon to do the printing and printing only and not translation. In connection with the important question that was asked by my hon. friend from Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) in regard to this new position of Assistant King's Printer, the Secretary of State very courteously replied to the question, but he did not give my hon. friend very much information with the result that the curiosity of my hon. friend has not been entirely satisfied. Is it the intention to fill this position by promotion in the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
The matter has only recently been considered in consequence



of the illness and death of Mr. Par-melee. As my hon. friend knows, the names which have been mentioned are names of men not at present employed in the Printing Bureau.
I am asking the hon. gentleman if, when he comes to fill the position, he will fill it by the promotion of some person employed in the Printing Bureau?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I am not sure. Personally I would like to fill that position, but I do not know yet whether there will be a promotion or not. This part of the question has not been considered yet. I will, of course, try to do what I think best in the interest of the Bureau. There are employees at the head of branches who are doing pretty well as heads of these branches. I do not know that they will be competent to fill the position of King's Printer. The position would require something more than that a man be simply an accountant, he would have to be a man of administrative ability. The question should remain in abeyance for a few days.
Until after the session.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: No, but the matter will have to remain in abeyance for a short time.
Will the appointment be made by the Civil Service Commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: It will have to be made according to law by the Civil Service Commissioners.
That is, 'the candidates will have to pass an examination?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I do not know. Whatever the law requires will be done.

The law requires that
every person has to pass an examination before being recommended by the Civil Service Commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I believe in this case, being a technical position, no examination would be required. The Civil Service Commission could issue a certificate according to Clause 21 of the Act, and in that case I do not think they would be obliged to hold a competitive examination.

I was pleased to hear my hon. friend the minister, in answer to my hon. friend (Mr. Murphy), say that the appointment would be made only in regard to the ability of the man to fill the position. Will my hon. friend follow that course?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Yes, I am in earnest.

I hope my hon. friend will carry out what he says, because that is the spirit I would like to see engendered in the public service. If he found that he had not a man in his department able to fill the position from an administrative standpoint, if he took in some one from the outside and made the appointment purely and simply in the interest of the department, to further the organization of his department and to better his department, I think I would be perfectly satisfied, because that is the spirit that should predominate. When I first asked my hon. friend the question, he told me that it was necessary to have an assistant because the work was so great. If it is necessary to have an assistant in a great department of that kind, the appointee of course would have to have some knowledge of printing, but the principle recommendation should be his powers of organization and administration. From such a large department my hon. friend surely could get some poor fellow who had earned his advance and could give him a step up in the world.
Is it the policy of the minister to promote employees who are qualified, provided the interests of his department are properly safeguarded?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Yes, it is the policy of the department and numerous proofs of this have already been given, in the Estimates of last year and in the Estimates of this year. From a perusal of these Estimates my hon. friend will see many promotions.
Many increases.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Yes, the statutory increases. I cannot do more than that.

Is there in the Printing Bureau a separate staff for the printing of French? Have you a certain number of men employed to print the French versions of the various documents, such as the Debates of the House or the Votes and Proceedings; or have you got a common staff with a number of men who can do the work in French and English and who, when they are not required to print French, are shifted into the English department?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
All the men employed
there can do both.
All the men employed in the Printing Bureau understand both French and English and are able to do the work in either French or English?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Yes, they are able to do the work in either French or English.
Is that one of the qualifications of employment in the Printing Bureau?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The work done there is done by the men, whether it is French or English.

Is the French work done by English printers who do not know French? Take the French version of
Hansard.' Does the minister mean to say that an English printer who knows no French at all is asked to print the French version of ' Hansard?'

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
No, I do not want to
say that. There are employees there who can speak French and English. I believe the Superintendent of Printing is a man wise enough to give the French ' Hansard ' to an employee who understands French. As a matter of fact, there is no such division as the one mentioned by my hon. friend; there is no special French or English staS. The Superintendent of Printing divides the work among the men according to what they know. If the work to be printed is French, the Superintendent of Printing gives that work to a man who understands French, and vice versa.

Have you any men in
the Printing Bureau who can print both French and English; that is, who know both the French and English languages? You say the Superintendent of Printing is a wise man. I do not believe that any wise man would give English copy to a Frenchman who did not know a word of English, or give French copy to an Englishman who did not know a word of French. Have you any men who can print in French, but cannot print in English, because they do not know the English language and have you any men who can print in English but cannot print in French because they do not know the French language?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Do you want to know
if all the employees can speak both languages and can therefore print in both languages?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I could not answer that now. If my hon. friend will give me time, I will make the necessary investigation.

If you have any French printers who can print both languages, when work is not sufficient to keep them 47i
busy, do you switch them on to English printing in preference to employees who know only one language and can only print in one language, or do yoti dispense with their services for the time being and keep men on who know only one language in preference to those who know two?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Personally, I do not
know what the Superintendent of Printing does in such cases. I know that he has been following the rules which have been in existence for many years.
What are the rules? I want to know if a man who knows both languages has the preference, when work diminishes and somebody has to be laid off, over a man who knows only one language,

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I do not believe that such a preference has been given, or that occasion for it has arisen, for the number of employees there, instead of decreasing, is always increasing. There is always work for the employees there.
Do I understand the minister to say that men employed during the session remain the year round?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Yes, I do not know of any dismissals, nor any decrease in the work.
Does not the printing of 'Hansard' and other sessional documents mean more work during the session?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
And are no extra men employed?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I do not know of any temporary employees.
During the session they run the Bureau at night as well as by day.
But the men do not work twenty-four hours a day. Among the temporary employees for the session, do you make a discrimination, giving the preference to the men who know both languages?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The occasion for such preference has never presented itself. There is plenty of work.
Not for the temporary men?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: There are none.

The hon. gentleman said there were.
Mr.* CODERRE: No, I said there were not -any. The employees who work at night during the session work during the day out of session.
Does the minister employ the same number of men the year round?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Of course during the session they do the work that is urgent, and other work is set aside. At the end of the session there is an accumulation of work to keep all hands busy.
That is a very ambiguous answer to a plain question. Does the minister employ the same number of men the year round?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: No, because the number is always increasing.
But does the minister keep them the year round?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I have not found any
men who wish to- leave, and personally I have no desire to send them away.

It is not a question of
what the men wish or what the minister desires. It is clear that during the session there is an extra amount of work. I ask if -the same number of men are employed the year round, and the minister tells me that the number goes on increasing. What is the proportion of that increase?-five, six, seven a month?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I cannot say offhand. Mr. BUREAU:	Could not the minister
give it in general terms?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I could bring all these
details at a later date.
If there are more Estimates for this department I would like to have these details.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, there will be more.
Civil Government-The Department of the Public Archives-Salaries, $o3,800 , contingencies, $7,500.

How many officers are
there in the Archives and what do they do?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: There are twenty-seven, -and they copy public documents and care for the collection already made.
Have you any employed outside?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Yes, two in England and three in Paris.
Who are in Paris?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Beauchene, Mr. Buron and Mr. Dugas. I believe _ that a young man named Morin has received an appointment recently, but I do not know that he is there yet.
What do you pay copyists?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Some of them $50 a
month.
Who are the copyists in England? 1

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Biggar and Mr. French. Mr. -Biggar has been there for years, hut Mr. French is a young Montrealer who was sent there a few months ago.
Are any employed in the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I believe that a few
months ago a young man named Lanctot was sent to California for special work.

A commission was
appointed some time ago to make an inspection of the departments with a view to collecting documents which could properly be added to the Archives. Has that commission reported?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Not yet.

I see the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) in his place, -and I desire to call his attention to the Archives. Would it not be well for him to consider the advisability o.f erecting a new building for the Archives, or at least enlarging the present one? I understand that -a delegation waited upon -him some time to urge the necessity of enlarging that building.
As a matter of fact, having occasion to frequent the building quite often, I know that it is impossible to accommodate all the documents within the four walls of the present building. The building is very unsuitable, and in view of the importance of the Archives Department, I think it should be enlarged, and be of a more imposing nature. Has the Minister of Public Works considered this matter, and if so, what does he intend to do about it ?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
When I had the pleasure of meeting the deputation to which my hon. friend refers, this matter was discussed, and the idea put forward by the deputation was that in the event of the

construction of a new building for the archives, which was deemed to be necessary, it should be constructed on the lower end of the property recently purchased on Wellington street. Nothing further than that has taken place.

I wish to call the attention of the minister to the fact that the copyists in London and Paris are paid only $50 a month. Generally the young men employed in that work are students. This employment does not last for many years, but during the time they are employed by the Dominion Government they should at least be paid a reasonable salary. $50 a month in Paris or London is certainly not a living allowance, and it should be doubled.
Progress reported.
On motion of Mr. Rogers, the House adjourned at 10.42 p.m.
Friday, February 13, 1914.
